## Essential Problem

The essential problem is the high water and energy consumption in the bathroom, which the user wants to reduce.

## Relevant Information

To address this problem, we need to consider various aspects of water and energy use in the bathroom:

**Water Use:**

* **Showering:** This is typically the biggest water guzzler in the bathroom.
* **Bathing:** While less common than showering, baths also use a significant amount of water.
* **Toilet flushing:** Each flush uses several gallons of water.
* **Handwashing and brushing teeth:** Leaving the tap running while washing hands or brushing teeth wastes water.
* **Leaks:** Even small leaks can waste gallons of water daily.

**Energy Use:**

* **Water heating:** Heating water for showers, baths, and handwashing consumes a lot of energy.
* **Lighting:** Bathroom lighting can be a significant energy drain.
* **Ventilation fans:** Running the fan for extended periods uses energy.

## Addressing the Problem

Here are some tips on how to reduce water and energy use in the bathroom:

**Water Conservation:**

* **Shorter showers:** Aim for 5-minute showers instead of longer ones.
* **Install a low-flow showerhead:** This can reduce water use by up to 50%.
* **Take baths less often:** Opt for showers whenever possible.
* **Install a dual-flush toilet:** This allows for a half-flush for liquid waste, saving water.
* **Turn off the tap while brushing teeth or shaving:** Don't let the water run unnecessarily.
* **Fix leaks promptly:** Even small leaks can waste gallons of water.
* **Collect cold water while waiting for it to heat up:** Use this water for watering plants or other purposes.

**Energy Conservation:**

* **Install a water heater timer:** This allows you to set specific times for water heating, reducing energy use when not needed.
* **Insulate your water heater:** This helps maintain the water temperature and reduces energy consumption.
* **Use LED light bulbs:** These are much more energy-efficient than traditional incandescent bulbs.
* **Turn off lights when not needed:** Make sure to switch off lights when leaving the bathroom.
* **Use natural light whenever possible:** Open windows and blinds to let in natural light.
* **Install a ventilation fan with a timer:** This ensures the fan doesn't run longer than necessary.
* **Consider a tankless water heater:** These heat water on demand, eliminating standby energy loss.

## Additional Tips

* **Educate everyone in your household about water and energy conservation:** Encourage everyone to adopt these practices.
* **Invest in water-saving appliances:** Look for toilets, showerheads, and washing machines with high water efficiency ratings.
* **Check your local water and energy provider websites for rebates and incentives:** You may be eligible for financial assistance for implementing water and energy-saving measures.

By following these tips, you can significantly reduce your water and energy consumption in the bathroom, saving money and helping the environment. Remember, every little bit counts!
gold_answer:
Others have already suggested [ low flow fixtures
](https://sustainability.stackexchange.com/a/9920/3379) and [ reducing water
usage ](https://sustainability.stackexchange.com/a/9919/3379) , but here are a
few other ideas, from least to most expensive:

  1. **Turn down your water heater.** The U.S. Department of Energy [ recommends a setting of ~120 F / 50 C ](https://www.energy.gov/energysaver/services/do-it-yourself-energy-savings-projects/savings-project-lower-water-heating) . Many water heaters are set at the factory to 140 F / 60 C, which can increase the standby losses (energy spent keeping the water in the tank hot) up to 20% annually. You may find you need to mix in less hot water at the shower or sink, which reduces your usage as well. Note that anything lower than the recommended setting may increase your risk of [ Legionnaire's disease ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legionnaires%27_disease#Reservoirs) . 
  2. **Insulate your hot water pipes.** Using [ pipe insulation ](https://www.homedepot.com/b/Plumbing-Pipe-Insulation/N-5yc1vZbuy9) on your hot water lines can result in savings of up to 4% annually, [ according to the DOE ](https://www.energy.gov/energysaver/services/do-it-yourself-energy-savings-projects/savings-project-insulate-hot-water-pipes) . 
  3. **Insulate your hot water heater.** If the heater is warm to the touch, you may benefit from adding a [ water heater blanket ](https://www.homedepot.com/s/water%2520heater%2520blanket?NCNI-5) . Note that most modern hot water heaters have well-insulated tanks, and older water heaters only last 10 to 15 years, so this is unlikely to be a necessary upgrade (i.e., if your water heater is old enough to benefit from this, you might be better off saving your money for the imminent replacement water heater). 
  4. **Install a "Shower Start" shower-head.** [ Shower Start TSV ](https://www.thinkevolve.com/pages/showerstart-tsv) (no affiliation) is a special showerhead that reduces flow to a trickle when hot water arrives at the fixture. This way, you turn on the showerhead and collect the cold water with a bucket (for watering plants, flushing toilets, etc). When the flow reduces, you move the bucket and pull the lanyard to start your shower with warm water. 
  5. **Install a recirculating pump.** A retrofit recirculating pump is typically installed under the sink in the bathroom farthest (by pipe run length) from the water heater. The system works by pumping water from the hot water pipes into the cold water pipes, shutting off with a thermostat, so that water at the tap is hot when you open it. Older systems, intended to improve comfort, ran continually, or on a timer (keeping them on in the morning and evening), which wasted a lot of energy. There are now [ on demand systems ](https://www.plumbingsupply.com/on-demand-recirculating-pumps.html) with a push-button -- you simply press the button a few minutes before you want to shower. The pump does use energy, but it saves water, and reduces the chance of hot water going down the drain (since you can get right in the shower after turning it on, rather than waiting too long for the water to be hot). Note that they are relatively expensive, so probably not a good choice unless you have a large house or a lot of people taking showers with long gaps in between.
